title: China's Proposed Solar Tech Export Curbs Expose India's Dependence on Factory Machinery
excerpt: Beijing's draft catalogue would prohibit or restrict exports of 12 solar manufacturing technologies, from perovskite cells to polysilicon processes, with public comment open until November 15. The products India buys would keep flowing; the machinery and know-how to make them at home are what is being gated.
body:
• China's commerce and science ministries proposed on October 16 adding 12 solar photovoltaic manufacturing technologies to the catalogue of technologies prohibited or restricted from export; public consultation runs until November 15, 2026.
  • Proposed prohibitions cover perovskite and perovskite-silicon tandem cell processes, wafers 70 micrometres or thinner, and large-scale fluidised-bed polysilicon production; TOPCon, HJT and back-contact cell processes would be restricted, meaning licensed, not banned.
  • A temporary pre-export registration requirement for the listed technologies has applied since October 16, even while the catalogue itself is still a draft.
  • The controls target manufacturing technology and know-how, not finished modules: India can keep buying Chinese panels, but building its own advanced factories gets harder.

China has proposed prohibiting or restricting exports of 12 solar photovoltaic manufacturing technologies, in a draft revision of its export catalogue that goes to the layer of the industry India most depends on: the machinery and process knowledge needed to build factories, rather than the panels those factories produce. The Ministry of Commerce and the Ministry of Science and Technology issued the proposal, Announcement No. 48 of 2026, on October 16, Energetica India reported. The draft covers 40 technologies in all: 23 in artificial intelligence, five in biomedicine and 12 in solar PV.

What Would Be Prohibited, and What Merely Licensed

On the prohibited side, the draft lists manufacturing processes for perovskite solar cells and perovskite-silicon tandem cells, including tandem production on wafers of at least 182 mm reaching conversion efficiencies of 30 percent or higher, silicon wafers 70 micrometres or thinner, and large-scale fluidised-bed polysilicon production, pv magazine reported. On the restricted side, where exports would need government approval and licences, sit high-efficiency crystalline-silicon processes: TOPCon, heterojunction (HJT) and back-contact cells, plus polysilicon plant engineering for lines of at least 30,000 tonnes a year.

Separately from the draft, a temporary registration requirement took effect on October 16: exporters of the listed technologies must register transactions with the commerce ministry before proceeding, including transfers already under way but not completed. The prohibitions and restrictions themselves have not taken effect; consultation closes November 15, and the final catalogue will decide the thresholds and procedures.

Why This Lands on India

The distinction that matters is products versus capability. As the Observer Research Foundation's analysis puts it, Chinese solar panels and cells will continue to sell; what Beijing is gating is the transfer of the underlying know-how, the process recipes and production lines that would let another country replicate Chinese capacity. Countries pursuing a China-plus-one strategy, India among them with its production-linked incentive schemes in solar and electronics, depend on importing exactly that layer: not just components, but equipment, process knowledge and the engineers who commission factories. Restrict it, the analysis argues, and the plus-one factory remains dependent rather than becoming a competitor.

China's weight in the chain is the reason the gate matters. Industry reporting on the proposal puts China at 75 to 95 percent of the global solar supply chain, including about 91 percent of polysilicon and over 97 percent of wafers. India's module assembly has scaled quickly under the PLI scheme, but its cell, wafer and equipment layers remain import-dependent, which is precisely the dependence the Moneycontrol reporting behind this story highlighted for solar and battery manufacturing machinery alike.

What Happens Next

The consultation closes on November 15, 2026. After that, the final catalogue will show which of the 12 solar technologies end up prohibited, which restricted, and on what thresholds. Indian manufacturers with factory projects in flight will be watching two things: whether equipment already contracted counts as a transfer that must be registered, and whether licensing, where it applies, is granted at a pace that keeps Indian cell and wafer projects on schedule. Until the final text lands, the honest position is that this is a proposal with an interim registration regime already running, not yet a ban.
